analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder for retirement plan participants to sue over self-dealing or conflicted transactions.
analysis.headline: The House Education and Workforce Committee voted 19-13 on March 17, 2026 to advance the bill, but it has not yet reached the House floor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raises the bar for workers who sue over their retirement plans. Under federal benefits law, workers can sue plan fiduciaries—the people and firms who manage 401(k)-type plans—for transactions the law prohibits, like self-dealing with parties who have a conflict of interest. This bill requires a plaintiff to prove up front that the transaction wasn't legally excused, before they can get documents and testimony through discovery. It also freezes discovery while a judge decides whether the case should be dismissed, with rules requiring the other side to preserve documents during that freeze.
analysis.who_benefits: Firms that administer and manage retirement plans—recordkeepers, asset managers, and plan fiduciaries—benefit because fewer fee and self-dealing lawsuits survive the early stages, and cases that do move forward are slower and cheaper to defend. Employers who sponsor plans and serve as fiduciaries also face less litigation exposure.

how_it_helps.text: For lawsuits alleging prohibited transactions with conflicted parties, the bill puts the burden on the plaintiff to plausibly allege and prove that the transaction is not exempt under ERISA's safe-harbor provision (Section 408(b)(2)), rather than letting the case proceed and testing that question later [S2].
For lawsuits involving the purchase or sale of employer securities, plaintiffs must plausibly allege and prove the transaction is not exempt under Section 408(e) [S2].

The bill stays all discovery and other proceedings while a motion to dismiss is pending, unless a court finds particularized discovery is needed to preserve evidence or prevent prejudice, so defendants face no document demands or depositions in the earliest phase of a case [S2].

To balance that freeze, the bill requires parties aware of the allegations to preserve relevant documents—including records held by custodians like recordkeepers—as if under a standing document request, with sanctions available for willful non-compliance [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Workers whose retirement savings sit in these plans bear the cost. Many meritorious claims about excessive fees or conflicted transactions depend on records the plan holders—such as fee documents, revenue-sharing agreements, and internal deliberations—do not have before discovery. If those claims die at the pleading stage, workers lose a way to recover losses from their retirement accounts, and plan misconduct faces less of a deterrent.

drawbacks.text: The pleading burden shift is likely to end many cases before plaintiffs can obtain the plan records needed to show a transaction was conflicted or excessively compensated, since those records are typically in the defendant's hands [S2].
The discovery stay delays cases for months or years while dismissal motions are briefed, reducing pressure on defendants to settle legitimate claims [S2].

The good-faith objection supporters would raise: excessive fiduciary-breach litigation raises plan administration costs and can make fiduciaries defensive, and a higher pleading bar filters weak suits earlier. An honest supporter would also acknowledge that the discovery stay, even with preservation duties, slows cases with strong facts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's costs fall on a diffuse group—tens of millions of retirement savers—while its benefits are concentrated on the firms that run those plans, which is why the balance tips against ordinary people. The preservation-and-sanctions provision shows drafters anticipated the evidence problem the stay creates, but a sanction after documents are gone does not undo a case dismissed for lack of proof.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House Education and Workforce Committee on a 19-13 vote in March 2026, but no floor vote has happened yet, so it is still moving through the process.

narrative.text: Rep. Randy Fine (R-FL) introduced the bill on November 18, 2025, and it was referred to both the Education and Workforce Committee and the Judiciary Committee [S1][S4].
On March 17, 2026, the committee held a markup session and voted 19-13 to order the bill reported as amended [S4].
As of the record provided, the bill has not received a vote in the full House [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, retirement plan administrators and fiduciaries are better off: the bill would cut their litigation exposure over fees and self-dealing, and it is advancing through the House without opposition from any Democratic cosponsor.

industries.industry: Retirement plan recordkeepers and asset managers
industries.note: These firms are the most frequent defendants in fiduciary-breach suits over fees and revenue sharing. The pleading shift and discovery stay make those suits harder to bring and win, which protects their revenue at the direct expense of workers whose plan fees are at issue.
Sponsor-employers and their officers face less exposure to suits over conflicted transactions and employer stock purchases, shifting the risk of fiduciary mistakes onto plan participants.

industries.industry: Class-action plaintiffs' firms handling ERISA cases
industries.note: Fewer fiduciary cases survive the pleading stage and those that do move more slowly, shrinking this practice area. Their loss tracks the loss of a remedy for workers.

analysis.trajectory: Bills that clear committee with a narrow 19-13 vote and a single cosponsor often wait for floor time under expedited procedures or a larger bill vehicle. With House Republicans holding a slim 223-217 majority, a procedural bill like this could reach the floor, but the record shows no scheduling so far, and it would then need to clear the Senate, where its fate is unknown.
